quests.correctSentence: Subject: Meeting Update  Hi team, the meeting has been moved to 3 pm due to a scheduling conflict.
quests.contrastSentence: Subject: Meeting Update  Hi team, the meeting is being moved to 3 pm due to a scheduling conflict.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Has been moved' is present perfect passive, connecting a recent change to its current effect: the meeting has been moved (and is now at 3 pm).
quests.nativeTip: The email is announcing a change that is now in effect.

quests.correctSentence: Hi Sam, could you let me know when you'll be free to review the draft?
quests.contrastSentence: Hi Sam, could you let me know that you'll be free to review the draft?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Let me know when' introduces an indirect question as a noun clause, a common structure in workplace messages asking for availability.
quests.nativeTip: This introduces an indirect question about time inside a polite request.

quests.correctSentence: Thanks for your patience. Should any issues come up, please don't hesitate to reach out.
quests.contrastSentence: Thanks for your patience. Would any issues come up, please don't hesitate to reach out.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should any issues come up' is a formal inverted conditional, commonly used in professional emails to sound polished and polite.
quests.nativeTip: This is the formal, inverted way of saying 'if any issues come up'.

quests.correctSentence: Traveler at check-in: Excuse me, could you tell me which gate is for flight 220?
quests.contrastSentence: Traveler at check-in: Excuse me, do you tell me which gate is for flight 220?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Could you tell me' is a polite, widely used request pattern for asking strangers for information in travel situations.
quests.nativeTip: This is a polite request to a stranger in a service setting.

quests.correctSentence: Airline staff: I'm sorry, but this flight is overbooked, so we need volunteers.
quests.contrastSentence: Airline staff: I'm sorry, but this flight was overbooked, so we need volunteers.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present simple passive describes a current state of affairs: the flight is overbooked, explaining what's happening right now.
quests.nativeTip: The staff member is describing the current situation at the gate.

quests.correctSentence: — How long have you been waiting at customs? — We have been standing here for over an hour.
quests.contrastSentence: — How long have you been waiting at customs? — We has been standing here for over an hour.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' takes 'have' in present perfect continuous: have been standing, emphasizing the ongoing wait right up to now.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'we' needs the matching present perfect continuous helper verb.

quests.correctSentence: Customer service chat: I understand your frustration. Your order will be shipped by tomorrow morning at the latest.
quests.contrastSentence: Customer service chat: I understand your frustration. Your order is shipped by tomorrow morning at the latest.
quests.ruleExplanation: Future passive reassures the customer about what will happen next: your order will be shipped, a common structure in customer service responses.
quests.nativeTip: This is a promise about a future action.

quests.correctSentence: — Can I get a refund for this item? — If the item is damaged, we can process a full refund.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can I get a refund for this item? — If the item was damaged, we can process a full refund.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a first conditional describing a real, checkable present condition: if the item is damaged, refund is possible. The if-clause stays in present simple.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a real, checkable condition about the present state of the item.

quests.correctSentence: — I never received a confirmation email. — I apologize for the inconvenience; let me look into that right away.
quests.contrastSentence: — I never received a confirmation email. — I apologize about the inconvenience; let me look into that right away.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Apologize for' is a fixed phrase; the preposition never changes regardless of context, unlike some other verb-preposition pairs.
quests.nativeTip: This fixed phrase always uses the same preposition.

quests.correctSentence: Interviewer: Tell me about a challenge you have overcome in your last role.
quests.contrastSentence: Interviewer: Tell me about a challenge you had overcome in your last role.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect fits questions about relevant past experience in interviews: challenges you have overcome, connecting past achievements to the present conversation.
quests.nativeTip: This asks about experience relevant to the interview happening now.

quests.correctSentence: Candidate: If I were hired, I would start by reviewing the current workflow.
quests.contrastSentence: Candidate: If I was hired, I would start by reviewing the current workflow.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If I were hired' uses the traditional second conditional form with 'were' for all subjects, common in interview answers about hypothetical scenarios.
quests.nativeTip: This is a hypothetical situation about a job offer that hasn't happened yet.

quests.correctSentence: Interviewer: Do you have any experience in managing remote teams?
quests.contrastSentence: Interviewer: Do you have any experience of managing remote teams?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Experience in' pairs naturally with a gerund: experience in managing, a standard interview phrase for describing skills.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective phrase pairs with a fixed preposition before a gerund.

quests.correctSentence: Doctor's office recording: If you are experiencing a medical emergency, please hang up and dial emergency services.
quests.contrastSentence: Doctor's office recording: If you is experiencing a medical emergency, please hang up and dial emergency services.
quests.ruleExplanation: First conditional with present continuous describes a real, current possibility: if you are experiencing, call for help immediately.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a real, ongoing possibility right now.

quests.correctSentence: Receptionist: Your appointment has been confirmed for Tuesday at 10 am.
quests.contrastSentence: Receptionist: Your appointment is being confirmed for Tuesday at 10 am.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect passive shows a completed action with present relevance: has been confirmed, meaning the appointment is set right now.
quests.nativeTip: The confirmation already happened and remains true now.

quests.correctSentence: — Can I reschedule my appointment? — Of course, which day works better for you?
quests.contrastSentence: — Can I reschedule my appointment? — Of course, what day works better for you?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' is often preferred over 'what' when choosing from a somewhat limited set of options, like days of the week.
quests.nativeTip: This question asks the patient to choose from a limited, implied set of days.

quests.correctSentence: Notice: All packages must not be left unattended in the lobby.
quests.contrastSentence: Notice: All packages mustn't have be left unattended in the lobby.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must not' expresses a firm prohibition suited to official notices: packages must not be left unattended, a clear rule with no exceptions.
quests.nativeTip: This is a strict rule, a clear prohibition.

quests.correctSentence: Notice: Residents are requested to keep noise to a minimum after 10 pm.
quests.contrastSentence: Notice: Residents is requested to keep noise to a minimum after 10 pm.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Are requested' fits this plural subject in a standing rule, a very common passive structure for polite official notices.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general, standing rule addressed to a plural group.

quests.correctSentence: Notice: This elevator is being serviced and will reopen this afternoon.
quests.contrastSentence: Notice: This elevator was being serviced and will reopen this afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present continuous passive describes an action happening right now: is being serviced, explaining the elevator's current unavailability.
quests.nativeTip: This describes work in progress at this exact moment.

quests.correctSentence: Form instructions: Applicants must complete every section before submitting.
quests.contrastSentence: Form instructions: Applicants might complete every section before submitting.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must' expresses a firm requirement typical of form instructions: must complete every section, with no exceptions allowed.
quests.nativeTip: This is a strict requirement on an official form.

quests.correctSentence: Form instructions: If any information is missing, your application will be returned.
quests.contrastSentence: Form instructions: If any information is missing, your application would be returned.
quests.ruleExplanation: First conditional describes the predictable result of missing information: will be returned, a standard structure in form instructions.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a real, predictable consequence of a real condition.

quests.correctSentence: — Do I need to sign every page? — Only the pages that are marked with an X.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do I need to sign every page? — Only the pages who are marked with an X.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That are' introduces a defining relative clause identifying exactly which pages: the pages that are marked with an X, essential information for completing the form correctly.
quests.nativeTip: This identifies specific pages out of all the pages in the form.

quests.correctSentence: Text message: Running late, would you mind waiting five more minutes?
quests.contrastSentence: Text message: Running late, will you mind waiting five more minutes?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would you mind' is the fixed polite request pattern reviewed from Stage 5, natural even in a quick, casual text message.
quests.nativeTip: This is the fixed polite phrase for a casual but courteous request.

quests.conceptTitle: Everyday Messaging: Will for Spontaneous Decisions
quests.grammarRule: Everyday Messaging: Will for Spontaneous Decisions
quests.correctSentence: Text message: Can't talk now, but I will call you back as soon as I'm free.
quests.contrastSentence: Text message: Can't talk now, but I would call you back as soon as I'm free.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will' fits this spontaneous decision made at the moment of texting: will call you back, a natural everyday promise.
quests.nativeTip: This decision to call back is being made spontaneously, right now.

quests.correctSentence: — Are we still on for dinner tonight? — Yes, nothing will change unless something urgent comes up at work.
quests.contrastSentence: — Are we still on for dinner tonight? — Yes, nothing would change unless something urgent comes up at work.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Nothing will change unless' combines simple future with 'unless' to describe a firm plan with one exception, a natural pattern in everyday confirmations.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a realistic future plan with one possible exception.

quests.correctSentence: Class instructions: Students are required to submit their essays online before midnight.
quests.contrastSentence: Class instructions: Students require to submit their essays online before midnight.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Are required to' takes the infinitive: required to submit, a standard structure for describing academic obligations.
quests.nativeTip: This fixed passive phrase pairs with an infinitive.

quests.correctSentence: — What happens if I miss the deadline? — If you miss the deadline, you'll lose ten percent of your grade.
quests.contrastSentence: — What happens if I miss the deadline? — If you missed the deadline, you'll lose ten percent of your grade.
quests.ruleExplanation: First conditional describes a real academic consequence: if you miss the deadline, you'll lose points, keeping the if-clause in present simple.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a real, likely future possibility with a clear rule attached.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you finish the reading before class? — No, I hadn't finished it when the professor called on me.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you finish the reading before class? — No, I hadn't finished it until the professor called on me.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'When' introduces the interrupting past event, paired naturally with past perfect: hadn't finished when she called on me, a classic sequencing pattern.
quests.nativeTip: This past perfect sentence needs a word introducing the sudden interrupting moment.

quests.correctSentence: Social invitation: A few of us are getting together this weekend; want to join?
quests.contrastSentence: Social invitation: A few of us were getting together this weekend; want to join?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A few of us' is treated as plural, taking 'are': a few of us are getting together, a casual, friendly invitation.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'a few of us' behaves as a plural group.

quests.correctSentence: — Have you seen the new café downtown? — Not yet, but I've heard it has amazing coffee.
quests.contrastSentence: — Have you seen the new café downtown? — Not yet, but I've heard it have amazing coffee.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'It' takes 'has' for this general fact about the café: it has amazing coffee, describing an ongoing quality rather than a momentary action.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'it' refers back to the singular café.

quests.correctSentence: — What would you do if you could live anywhere? — Honestly, if money were no object, I'd move to the coast.
quests.contrastSentence: — What would you do if you could live anywhere? — Honestly, if money was no object, I'd move to the coast.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If money were no object' uses the traditional second conditional 'were', wrapping up this real-world block by returning to a structure first mastered back in Stage 7.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Levels 181–190 with the same hypothetical form of 'be' practiced throughout Stage 7.
